collection.title: Bovine H5N1 influenza viruses have adapted to more efficiently use receptors abundant in cattle
collection.authors: Hassard, J. A.; Yang, J.; Hawkins, D. E. D. P.; Pekar, J. E.; Dadonaite, B.; Yu, J.; Richardson, S. A. S.; Pinto, R. M.; Ramirez Valdez, K.; Lemey, P.; Quantrill, J. L.; Neil, C.; Adams, L.; Xue, J.; Ogando, N. S.; Masonou, T.; Case, K.-M.; Ajeian, J.; Woodall, M. N. J.; Ross, R. A.; Hudson, N.; Zhong, K.; Cao, H.; Jones, S.; Klim, H.; Wasik, B. R.; Dermawan, D. N.; Sadeyen, J.-R.; Werling, D.; Yaffy, D.; James, J.; Nunez, A.; Digard, P.; Brown, I. H.; Goldhill, D. H.; Murcia, P. R.; Smith, C. M.; Liu, Y.; Bloom, J. D.; Iqbal, M.; Barclay, W. S.; Haslam, S. M.; Peacock, T. P.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: The Pirbright Institute, Woking, Surrey, UK, GU24 0NF; Department of Infectious Disease, Imperial College London, UK, W2 1PG
collection.abstract: Sustained mammal-to-mammal transmission of high pathogenicity H5N1 avian influenza viruses is reshaping the host range of these pathogens. One of the longest-running mammalian transmission chains involves the B3.13 genotype circulating in U.S. dairy cattle which was detected in early 2024. Genomic analyses revealed selection and rapid fixation of haemagglutinin mutations D104G and V147M. We demonstrate, via glycomic profiling, that bovine tissues, including the mammary gland, are enriched in N- and O-linked glycans capped with N-glycolylneuraminic acid (NeuGc), a sialic acid which is not synthesised by humans and birds, which instead express only N-acetylneuraminic acid (NeuAc). Early cattle H5 viruses poorly recognised NeuGc, but D104G and V147M enabled efficient engagement of both NeuAc- and NeuGc-containing receptors. These mutations enhanced replication in bovine mammary tissue without major attenuation of replication in human lung and primary nasal epithelial cells. NeuGc-driven receptor adaptation therefore promotes viral fitness in cattle without majorly changing zoonotic risk. Deep mutational scanning was able to identify alternative haemagglutinin substitutions that confer NeuGc usage and represent surveillance markers for emerging cattle H5 lineages. Finally, structural analyses suggest a potential molecular mechanism for the dual binding of the cattle-adapted viruses.

collection.title: Inflammation-driven cellular selection impacts X-linked mosaicism in the epidermis
collection.authors: Angelopoulou, E.; Gandhi, K.; van Wolfswinkel, M.; Schmautz, L.; Oyarzun, I.; Nowosadtko, S.; Fischer, I.; Schwartz, V.; Griss, J. J.; Ellis, S. J.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: University of Vienna / Max Perutz Labs
collection.abstract: In eutherian females, the choice of which X chromosome gets embryonically inactivated is thought to be random. Somatic tissues are thus assumed to comprise cells with a 50:50 ratio of maternal:paternal X active. However, a phenomenon known as X-skewing has been observed, wherein tissue composition shifts to be dominated by cells expressing one X or the other. On a gross level, such X-skewing is phenotypically silent except in the case where one X-chromosome carries a disease mutation. Here, by leveraging a mouse model of an X-linked disease called Incontinentia Pigmenti, caused by heterozygous mutations in the NF-kB effector, Nemo, we explore how X-linked cellular dynamics shape progenitor biology in the epidermis. Lineage tracing with X-linked reporters shows that at birth, the epidermis is unexpectedly skewed toward mutant cells. Within a week, as inflammation emerges, these dynamics reverse leaving surviving animals with almost entirely wild-type epithelium. The shift is driven by loss rather than growth since mutant cells adopt an aberrant fate and die at higher rates than their wild-type neighbours; proliferation rises in both populations. Notably, wild-type proliferation scales with local tissue composition, suggesting these cells calibrate their response to the extent of the mutant burden to compensate appropriately for tissue loss. Depleting macrophages, the principal TNF- source, attenuates inflammation, mutant cell death and ultimately is expected to preserve the mutant population. Altogether, our results identify inflammation as a selective force capable of resolving deleterious mosaicism, not only in the context of an X-linked disease, but within any dynamic, clonally heterogeneous epithelium.

collection.title: Contrasting relationships between evolved consumer diversity and productivity for essential vs. substitutable resources
collection.authors: Gopakumar, A.; Diehl, S.; Brännström, A.
collection.abstract: Any mechanistic biodiversity-ecosystem functioning theory must explain how biodiversity in natural communities arises, which requires an evolutionary metacommunity perspective. Using a model of adaptive evolution of competitive metacommunities in landscapes with spatially heterogeneous supply of two resources, we studied the evolution of resource-uptake specialization as a function of resource type (substitutable/essential) and trade-off shape between resource-uptake affinities (generalist-/specialist-favouring). We identified "critical essentiality" as a key phenomenon separating parameter regions with fundamentally different biodiversity--ecosystem function relationships. Specifically, while greater spatial heterogeneity in resource supply increases biodiversity, this comes at the cost of reduced productivity when resources are essential. Moreover, when resources are essential, both generalist- and specialist-favoring trade-offs select for phenotypes that prevent efficient resource partitioning, leading to low resource use efficiency and consumer biomass - despite often high species richness. In contrast, when resources are substitutable, a specialist-favoring affinity trade-off selects for phenotypes that partition resources efficiently, promoting a metacommunity of only two species characterized by high functional diversity, resource use efficiency, and biomass. Overall, our analyses thus suggest that conditions promoting the evolution of diverse consumer communities often do not engender higher functional richness, consumer biomass, or resource use efficiency.

collection.title: WildObserve: Camera-trap image review software that learns species labels during annotation
collection.abstract: Motion-activated camera traps are an effective tool for monitoring animals, but a single study can produce millions of images, which must be analyzed before they yield data. The burden of analyzing them has led many teams to automate the work with computer vision. These models lose accuracy on images unlike those they were trained on, however, and a general model may not use the categories a project needs. Adapting a model to a project usually requires at least one of the following: many labeled images per species, programming expertise, a graphics processing unit (GPU), or uploading images to a remote server. I describe WildObserve, a desktop application that adapts to each project without any of these requirements. Before a reviewer sees an image, MegaDetector finds animals, people, and vehicles and marks images that are likely empty, and SpeciesNet suggests a species for each animal. WildObserve keeps SpeciesNet's feature vector for each animal, so as the reviewer confirms or corrects labels, a project model (a logistic regression on those features) retrains in about a second on an ordinary laptop, learning the project's own species list and names. Images stay on the user's computer, model outputs and human decisions are kept separate, and exports record review and model provenance. On the Caltech Camera Traps dataset, WildObserve processed 8.1 images/s on an Apple M1 Pro laptop with Core ML (1.5 images/s on its CPU), species suggestions included. At a 0.5 threshold, it found animals in 97.1% of animal images but also put a box on 48.0% of images labeled empty. On 1,467 animal crops from 14 categories, SpeciesNet alone reached 0.919 balanced accuracy. The project model reached 0.886 with three labels per category and 0.937 with 25, and 0.931 on camera locations absent from its training labels; built on features from DINOv2, a general-purpose image model, it reached only 0.784 with 50. On the Oregon Critters dataset, released after SpeciesNet was trained, SpeciesNet reached 0.751 and the project model passed it with only ten labels per category (0.783). WildObserve gives a project species suggestions in its own categories, from a model it trains simply by reviewing, without writing code, needing a GPU, or sending images elsewhere.

collection.title: Rapid trait adaptation has contrasting effects on different dimensions of stability under environmental change
collection.authors: Holmes, M.; Yamamichi, M.; De Laender, F.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: BC3, Basque Centre for Climate Change
collection.abstract: Environmental change alters species growth rates and, through species interactions, can produce complex effects on community functioning and composition. Because functional traits mediate both environmental responses and competition, rapid trait adaptation may modify these effects, but its consequences in multispecies communities remain unclear. We used a trait-based model of competitive communities to test how adaptation affects the mean and diversity of species growth responses to environmental change, and how this influences functional and compositional resistance (how unaffected the community is by the environmental change) and resilience (how well it recovers after it has acclimated to the altered environment). Adaptation altered response variance more strongly than the mean by changing the balance between environmental optimisation and competition-driven trait divergence. As a result, adaptation strongly increased compositional stability, but had less clear effects on abundance. Adaptation also generated a trade-off between resistance and resilience: faster adaptation improved resistance but reduced resilience as communities were displaced less by the environmental change and thus recovered less. Overall, adaptation can be stabilising, but higher adaptation rates do not necessarily produce greater stability across all stability components.
